slides.title: Why multimodal eval is hard
slides.body:
Single-modality eval has well-trodden paths: ImageNet for image classification, GLUE/MMLU for language, WER for speech. Multimodal eval is messier because:

1. **There's often no single correct answer.** 'What's happening in this image?' has many valid descriptions.
2. **Failure modes are subtle.** A model that hallucinates objects passes most automatic metrics. A model that's correctly grounded but verbose loses on length-sensitive scores.
3. **Benchmarks contaminate fast.** VQAv2, COCO captioning — both are old enough that frontier models have likely seen them in training.
4. **Modality-specific failures don't generalize.** Strong on VQA doesn't mean strong on document reading; strong on natural images doesn't mean strong on medical or scientific imagery.

This lesson covers the standard benchmark suites, where they fail, and how production teams supplement them with custom evaluations.

slides.title: The benchmark suite
slides.body:
**Standard benchmarks for VLMs**:

- **VQAv2**: open-ended visual question answering. ~250K image-question-answer triples. Image of dog → 'is the dog brown?' → 'yes'. Saturated; modern VLMs hit 85%+.
- **GQA**: compositional VQA (counting, relationships). Harder than VQAv2; less saturated.
- **TextVQA**: questions about text in images. Tests OCR + reasoning.
- **DocVQA / ChartQA**: document understanding. Critical for enterprise use cases.
- **MMMU**: multi-discipline understanding (medical, business, art). Designed to be uncontaminated; current frontier models around 70-80%.
- **MathVista**: math problems with visual context. Tests visual math reasoning.
- **MM-Vet**: 16 capability categories (recognition, OCR, knowledge, math, spatial). Capability matrix rather than aggregate score.
- **Hallucination benchmarks**: POPE (Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation) — does the model hallucinate non-existent objects? Critical safety metric.

For image generation:
- **FID / KID**: distance between generated and real image distributions. Standard but blunt.
- **CLIP score**: how well the generated image matches the prompt (CLIP embedding similarity).
- **Human eval**: pairwise preference. Slow + expensive; the only way to measure real quality.

For speech:
- **WER (word error rate)**: standard for ASR.
- **MOS (mean opinion score)**: standard for TTS naturalness; requires human annotators.

slides.title: Hallucination — the dominant failure mode
slides.body:
VLMs hallucinate. They describe objects that aren't in the image, count things that aren't there, attribute properties incorrectly. **Hallucination is the most important practical failure mode for multimodal models in production.**

Why it happens:
- Training data is web-scraped; captions often contain content not visible in the image (context, opinions, mentions of objects elsewhere). The model learns to generate similar 'plausible context' even when ungrounded.
- LLMs are pretrained to maximize fluency; visual grounding is a soft constraint added later via fine-tuning.
- Beam search / temperature sampling can amplify confident-but-wrong assertions.

**Detection methods**:

- **POPE**: ask 'is there a {object} in the image?' for objects in and not in the image. Compute precision/recall.
- **CHAIR**: count hallucinated objects in generated captions vs ground-truth annotations.
- **LLM-as-judge**: separate LLM compares generation to image; flags inconsistencies.
- **Object-grounded validation**: run a separate object detector; cross-reference with the VLM's claims.

**Mitigation**:
- Better training data (clean captions; remove context-only mentions).
- RLHF on hallucination preferences.
- Constrained decoding (e.g., RAG-style retrieval before generation).
- Smaller models are sometimes safer (less confident; harder to hallucinate fluently).

question.question: Why does benchmark contamination matter for multimodal evaluation specifically?
options: Multimodal benchmarks are easier to leak

Most multimodal benchmarks (VQAv2, COCO) are public and on the web. Models trained on web-scraped image-text data have likely seen the test images and the answers. Reported benchmark scores conflate generalization ability with memorization. Newer benchmarks (MMMU, MM-Vet, EgoSchema) are designed with contamination resistance — but they too will leak over time. The half-life of a clean benchmark is now measured in months
question.explanation: Web-scale data + public benchmarks = inevitable leakage. A frontier VLM training on 5B+ images has almost certainly seen VQAv2's images during pretraining. Scores on contaminated benchmarks measure memorization + generalization, not generalization alone. The whole field has moved toward private holdouts (vendor-specific evals) and frequently-refreshed public benchmarks. Treat all reported benchmark numbers with skepticism; trust your own held-out evaluation set.

slides.title: Production eval — beyond benchmarks
slides.body:
Production multimodal apps need more than aggregate benchmark scores. Three additional layers:

**1. Custom held-out set.** 100-500 examples curated for your specific task. Examples that exercise the failure modes you care about — your customers' edge cases, regulatory requirements, brand-specific rules. Run before every model update; track score over time.

**2. Online evaluation.** Sample 1-5% of production traffic; score with an LLM-as-judge or human review. Detects drift, deployment issues, regressions that don't show up offline.

**3. Adversarial probing.** Specific test cases for known failure modes:
- Hallucination probes (is there a non-existent object?).
- Refusal calibration (refuses harmful queries; doesn't over-refuse safe queries).
- Robustness (small image perturbations don't change answers; rotated/cropped images still work).
- Multi-image reasoning (compares two images; counts across a sequence).

**Metric design tips**:
- **Anti-cheating**: include 'unanswerable' questions to measure willingness-to-decline. Frontier models often answer everything; a strong VLM should refuse when the image doesn't support a claim.
- **Capability decomposition**: measure separately (perception, OCR, knowledge, reasoning, generation) rather than one score. A 70% aggregate can hide a 90% perception + 30% reasoning split.
- **Length normalization**: VLMs reward verbose outputs on automatic metrics. Length-normalize or use exact-match scoring on short answers.

slides.title: The end of the path
slides.body:
Multimodal models are the natural extension of LLMs to other modalities. The architecture story is largely settled (transformers + attention + appropriate encoders); the eval story is much messier.

For a team deploying multimodal: **measure your specific use case**. Public benchmarks are useful for tracking the field, but they're not your evaluation. Build a custom held-out set, log online eval, probe for hallucination explicitly, and treat reported leaderboard scores with skepticism.

The full multimodal toolkit you've built in this path:

- **Image foundations** + **Vision Transformers**: the substrate.
- **Contrastive learning** + **CLIP**: the joint embedding space.
- **Diffusion** + **text-to-image**: image generation.
- **Audio + speech**: the third modality.
- **Multimodal fusion**: how to combine modalities in different architectures.
- **Multimodal evaluation**: how to measure all of this.

This was the last lesson in the multimodal-engineer path. From [[image-foundations]] through evaluation, you've covered the full multimodal stack of modern ML.

Key takeaways:
- Standard benchmarks (VQAv2, COCO, MMMU) are useful but contaminated
- Hallucination is the dominant practical failure mode; measure with POPE/CHAIR
- Production needs: custom held-out + online eval + adversarial probing
- Decompose capabilities; don't trust aggregate scores
- The field is converging architecturally; eval is where the pain is
